title: Benchmark success: Average scores conceal complete-task failure
desc: Separates narrow capability, assistance and autonomous practice across tasks, configurations and citation-quality dimensions.

kps.k: The central dispute concerns what benchmark success establishes: narrow legal capability, useful assistance or dependable autonomous lawyering.
kps.d: The corpus moves beyond bar exams toward task-specific reasoning, professional work products and complete agentic assignments. LegalBench separates legal capabilities across 162 tasks; Allens and Linklaters test specialist legal questions; Harvey’s benchmarks extend to document-based work. These instruments measure different outcomes, not a common scale of lawyer replacement. Allens and Linklaters also lack matched human controls, so their lawyer-level grading standards do not establish direct comparative performance.

qs.q: These results emphasize that assessments of LLM capabilities for legal applications must be made on a task-by-task basis, and informed by the nuances of specific tasks.
qs.a: LegalBench: A Collaboratively Built Benchmark for Measuring Legal Reasoning in Large Language Models · Academia · 2023

qs.q: Human–lawyer benchmarking  Unlike other studies, our benchmark does not include a human-lawyer "control" benchmark.
qs.a: The 2025 Allens AI Australian law benchmark · Law firms · 2025

kps.k: Measured improvements coexist with persistent variation across tasks, jurisdictions and model configurations.
kps.d: Allens reports average substance scores rising from 1.92/5 in February 2024 testing to 4.3/5 in April 2025. LinksAI’s February 2025 update places o1 at 6.4/10 and Gemini 2.0 at 6.0/10, while finding weaker factual application and clause interpretation than summarisation. Neither newer models nor reasoning models lead every practice area. LegalBench’s American-law emphasis, Allens’ foreign-law intrusion findings and overlapping Thai model–student essay performance limit generalisation across jurisdictions.

qs.q: - The average *substance *score of all the LLMs we tested was higher in 2025 (4.3** out of **5**) than in 2024 (**1.92** out of **5**), confirming the overall improvement across the board through the year, including with the appearance of the new generation of reasoning models (such as DeepSeek and OpenAI o1).
qs.a: The 2025 Allens AI Australian law benchmark · Law firms · 2025

qs.q: In contrast, their ability to apply the law to the facts or interpret clauses is less good.
qs.a: The LinksAI English law benchmark (Version 2) · Law firms · 2025

kps.k: Direct human comparisons show genuine task-specific strengths without establishing general professional superiority.
kps.d: Better Call GPT reports GPT4-1106’s contract issue-determination F-score of 0.871, close to outsourced practitioners’ 0.874 and above juniors’ 0.860; weaker issue-location performance qualifies autonomous markup. Silicon Formalism reports perfect experimental legal compliance for GPT-5 and Gemini 3 Pro, exceeding judges, while two non-reasoning models underperform judges. These bounded findings challenge blanket incapability claims but do not resolve performance on unrestricted legal practice. Separately, re-evaluation places GPT-4 around the 48th percentile among bar passers and questions whether exam percentiles measure practical competence at all.

qs.q: Arguably, the lower performance by LLMs in locating issues could impact their ability to accurately mark up contracts on their own, constraining their effectiveness in eliminating the role of a Lawyer in contract review.
qs.a: Better Call GPT: Comparing Large Language Models Against Lawyers · Academia · 2024

kps.k: Complete-task grading reveals failures that high average or criterion-level scores can conceal.
kps.d: Harvey’s May 2026 LAB results put every evaluated frontier model below 10% end-to-end completion under an all-required-criteria standard. Artificial Analysis’s separate July 2026 LAB-AA implementation reports a leading 14.2% configuration, including a one-task fallback. Vals’ Legal Research Bench illustrates the metric distinction directly: Claude Opus 5 receives 90.58% weighted credit but 55.29% strict all-pass accuracy. These results concern different runs and tasks, not a directly comparable progress series. Legora instead heavily weights consequential omissions, reflecting a related but distinct risk-sensitive scoring choice.

qs.q: From this analysis, three meaningful trends have emerged:  -  Legal work is far from saturated by frontier models**: Under our strict all-pass standard, the frontier models we evaluated complete less than 10% of tasks end-to-end in aggregate.
qs.a: Initial Results on Legal Agent Benchmark: A First Look at Frontier Model Performance on Long-Horizon Legal-Agent Work · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: - Under partial-credit scoring, [Claude Opus 5](/models/anthropic_claude-opus-5) reaches 90.58% weighted pass rate but 55.29% under strict all-pass grading, where every rubric check must pass.
qs.a: Vals Index — Continuous Independent Agentic Benchmark (Legal Sector: Legal Research Bench + Independent HLAB Runs) · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

kps.k: Citation reliability requires more than authentic case names or fluent explanations.
kps.d: Large Legal Fictions reports 58–88% hallucination rates across its tested public models on pooled reference-based tasks. The separate Stanford RegLab legal-research study reports 17–33% under its broader measure covering incorrect information and false source support; it deliberately tests challenging queries and rejects population-wide interpretation. Allens distinguishes fabricated authorities from real foreign authorities wrongly applied, and its 23% absent-or-fabricated authority figure is not a fabrication-only rate. Who Checks the Citations finds that automated detection handles nonexistent cases better than pinpoint errors, misquotations and content misrepresentation. Bluebook formatting compliance is another separate capability, not a hallucination measure.

qs.q: Because legal research commonly requires the inclusion of citations, we define a hallucination as a response that contains either incorrect information or a false assertion that a source supports a proposition.
qs.a: Hallucination-Free? Assessing the Reliability of Leading AI Legal Research Tools · Academia · 2025

qs.q: Our best agent reliably detects non-existent cases and case name mismatches, but struggles with verifying pincites,6 misquotes, and content misrepresen- tations.
qs.a: Who Checks the Citations? Benchmarking Legal Hallucination Detection · Academia · 2026

kps.k: Specialisation, retrieval and prompting can improve performance, but none provides a general reliability guarantee.
kps.d: Harvey reports advantages on its own BigLaw Bench, while Descrybe’s vendor-run bar-question comparison reports 200/200 correct answers and 99.70% judge-scored reasoning. These claims require scrutiny of task selection, scoring and possible training exposure. Independent legal-RAG testing finds improvement without eliminating errors. Allens finds mixed effects from web access; Harvey reports that explicit sourcing prompts worsened foundation-model answers. The RAG Report describes qualitative long-context degradation, not a quantified universal comparison. General-purpose tests therefore cannot establish specialised-product performance, and specialised-product branding cannot establish dependable deployment.

qs.q: | System | Correct answers out of 200 | Rubric-scored reasoning quality | |---|---|---| | DescrybeLM | 200 (100%) | 99.70% | | ChatGPT 5.2 | 187 (93.5%) | 93.41% | | Claude Opus 4.5 | 177 (88.5%) | 89.03% | | Gemini 3 Pro | 184 (92.0%) | 91.45% |  *Rubric-scored reasoning quality reflects judge-model scoring; see Evaluation Approach within the white paper for methodology and limitations.
qs.a: AI Built For Law Outperforms ChatGPT, Claude, And Gemini On Legal Reasoning Benchmark · Market & press · 2026

qs.q: We find that legal RAG can reduce hallucinations compared to general-purpose AI systems (here, GPT-4), but hallucinations remain substantial, wide-ranging, and potentially insidious.
qs.a: Hallucination-Free? Assessing the Reliability of Leading AI Legal Research Tools · Academia · 2025

kps.k: Benchmark credibility depends on the evaluator as well as the evaluated model.
kps.d: Expert marking captures legal nuance but costs resources and can involve legitimate disagreement. LLM judges enable scale, yet agreement with experts is not equivalent to independent correctness. PRBench reports judge–expert agreement statistics, and LeMAJ claims improved correspondence without numerical detail in the supplied excerpt. The Thai grading study finds higher model-panel agreement than human-panel agreement because models converge on the majority interpretation and fail to reproduce a coherent minority reading. Prompt sensitivity, undisclosed configurations, possible test leakage and changing products further limit reproducibility. Internal inconsistencies in Allens’ citation rankings and the Thai pass count should remain unresolved rather than be silently repaired.

qs.q: While marking by expert legal practitioners is necessarily more resource-intensive than other automated or programmatic marking solutions, it has complemented Allens' broader adoption of LLMs across its existing legal practice and continues to facilitate an ongoing consideration of how such tools can be effectively and reliably used in day-to-day practice.
qs.a: The 2025 Allens AI Australian law benchmark · Law firms · 2025

qs.q: The high LLM-panel α reflects systematic convergence on the majority                                                   reading rather than balanced reproduction of both readings; a benchmark that selects its LLM judge                                                   by maximising agreement with a human reference panel will inherit this asymmetry by construction.
qs.a: A Two-Phase Stability Study of LLM Judges and Bar Council Examiners on Thai Bar-Exam Free-Form Essays · Academia · 2026

kps.k: Standalone output quality does not establish the benefit of giving humans AI assistance.
kps.d: AI Assistance in Legal Analysis finds improved straightforward multiple-choice performance but no meaningful average essay gain, with larger benefits for weaker students and possible harm to stronger students. It separately reports realistic-task experiments showing more consistent speed gains than quality gains. The Suffolk faculty memorandum reports a newer 137-student trial with quality gains on at least four of six tasks, suggesting that conclusions depend on tools and study conditions. Student samples do not establish effects for experienced practitioners, while field-study satisfaction and productivity reports remain subjective. The supplied AI-Powered Lawyering excerpt motivates a randomised trial but provides no results.

qs.q: We also found that access to GPT-4 improved average student performance only on straightforward multiple-choice questions, with essentially no change to performance on essay questions.
qs.a: AI Assistance in Legal Analysis: An Empirical Study · Academia · 2025

qs.q: At the same time, the primary limitation of these studies is their reliance on upper-level law students rather than practicing attorneys as study subjects.
qs.a: Thinking Like a Lawyer in the Age of Generative AI: Cognitive Limits on AI Adoption Among Lawyers · Academia · 2025

kps.k: Practical efficiency should include verification and correction, not merely generation speed or model cost.
kps.d: Better Call GPT reports substantially faster model processing and a 99.97% cost-reduction claim, although the supplied cost material does not establish its full calculation. At the other end, Harvey reports roughly $50 and more than 20 minutes per task at LAB’s frontier. Vals finds that more tool calls, citations and words do not reliably yield better answers. The Victorian census report identifies time to an acceptable quality threshold as an unmeasured practical outcome; Thinking Like a Lawyer notes that verification can sometimes cost more effort than independent production. These qualifications support workflow-level testing rather than inference from leaderboard scores alone.

qs.q: The longest processing time was taken by GPT-1106 at an average of 4.7 minutes and the shortest Palm2 text-bison at 0.73 minutes.
qs.a: Better Call GPT: Comparing Large Language Models Against Lawyers · Academia · 2024

qs.q: On LAB, reaching the top of the leaderboard runs to roughly $50 per task and over 20 minutes of latency.
qs.a: Initial Results on Legal Agent Benchmark: A First Look at Frontier Model Performance on Long-Horizon Legal-Agent Work · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

kps.k: Sources disagree over the implications for replacement more than over the existence of useful capabilities.
kps.d: Allens predicts enduring strategic human roles and argues that more training alone will not resolve fundamental limitations. A View of How Language Models Will Transform Law instead anticipates mature systems handling routine services with minimal supervision; its projected 95.7% reasoning accuracy is hypothetical. Better Call GPT’s disruption rhetoric also exceeds its qualified task results. Thinking Like a Lawyer interprets mixed methods as evidence of transformative capacity, while practitioner accounts stress unresolved novelty, ambiguity and argument development. These are competing interpretations and conditional forecasts, not measured employment outcomes or proof of permanent technical limits.

qs.q: These limitations are unlikely to be solved by simply adding more data or training—they stem from how LLMs work.
qs.a: The 2025 Allens AI Australian law benchmark · Law firms · 2025

qs.q: - Working with the *aid *of such tools, as opposed to being replaced by them, is the likely outcome for lawyers in this rapidly evolving dynamic, where the promise of AI-backed efficiencies should allow lawyers to focus on more strategic issues instead of simple questions of fact.
qs.a: Lawyer or language model? Testing AI's competence in answering Australian legal questions (The Allens AI Australian Law Benchmark) · Law firms · 2024

kps.k: The shared operational implication is supervised, task-specific adoption backed by transparent testing.
kps.d: Allens, the legal-research reliability study and litigation guidance recommend checking substantive accuracy, source support, currency, completeness and jurisdiction before reliance. Continuous model monitoring does not replace verification of individual work products. Public evaluation and representative testing matter particularly where lay users or small organisations lack expertise to detect persuasive errors. Narrow applications may still help: Getting in the Door reports encouraging attorney satisfaction for minimum-eligibility screening that routes applicants to human intake, while acknowledging missing follow-up questions, censorship and bias risks. Neither enterprise adoption nor favourable intake feedback establishes a reduction in unmet legal need.

qs.q: Users of these tools must continue to verify that key propositions are accurately supported by citations.
qs.a: Hallucination-Free? Assessing the Reliability of Leading AI Legal Research Tools · Academia · 2025

qs.q: We suspect that the goal of our expert rater, who is a supervising attorney, to obtain detailed information from the appli- cant to use in making a final representation decision, may not have perfectly matched the design of our system, which was to assess the minimum standard for eligibility, in order to get an applicant who may qualify to a human for a full intake as efficiently as possible.
qs.a: Getting in the Door: Streamlining Intake in Civil Legal Services with Large Language Models · Academia · 2024

vlens.an: The curated academia-and-research sources broadly accept the proposition that benchmark averages establish bounded capabilities, not dependable end-to-end lawyering, and materially develop it through more granular evaluation methods. Common reasons include substantial variation by task, model, prompt and jurisdiction; persistent hallucinations and incomplete answers despite retrieval or specialisation; weaker performance on complex reasoning than on mechanical tasks; uncertainty about whether standalone output improves human performance; verification costs; and concerns about evaluator validity. Several studies extend the proposition by separately benchmarking procedural citation compliance, citation-error detection and LLM judging, showing that aggregate accuracy or high evaluator agreement can conceal distinct failures such as noncompliant citations, missed misquotations and loss of legitimate minority interpretations. Internal variation is material: some sources forecast routine-work substitution or wider market transformation, but generally treat those as conditional predictions rather than present evidence of autonomous reliability; others support narrow supervised applications such as legal-aid screening or propose verification-oriented agents. One source redirects attention toward unequal access-to-justice benefits, while technical overviews that merely invoke bar-exam performance or recommend specialised systems provide insufficient evidence on complete-task reliability. Thus this professional voice not only supports the synthesis’s caution but strengthens it by identifying additional dimensions and methodological mechanisms through which headline scores can mislead.

qs.q: These results emphasize that assessments of LLM capabilities for legal applications must be made on a task-by-task basis, and informed by the nuances of specific tasks.
qs.a: LegalBench: A Collaboratively Built Benchmark for Measuring Legal Reasoning in Large Language Models · Academia · 2023

qs.q: We show (1) that these models produce fully compliant Bluebook citations only 69%-74% of the time and (2) that in-context learning on the Bluebook’s underlying system of rules only raises accuracy to 77%.
qs.a: Bye-bye, Bluebook? Automating Legal Procedure with Large Language Models · Academia · 2025

vlens.an: The curated legal-tech vendor sources accept the proposition that aggregate benchmark success does not establish dependable completion of legal work and materially develop it through concrete evaluation methods. Their common reasoning is that legal deliverables can fail because of a single consequential omission; performance varies by task, practice area, model configuration and task length; and benchmark credibility depends on grading design as well as model output. Harvey’s LAB and Vals provide the clearest direct evidence by separating high criterion-level or weighted performance from much lower strict all-pass completion. Legora adds risk-weighted scoring rather than a purely binary threshold, while Harvey’s BigLaw Bench distinguishes useful drafting assistance from complete professional coverage. PRBench and LeMAJ extend the evaluator side through criterion-level analysis, judge–expert agreement and granular assessment, but do not test end-to-end completion. Harvey also reports improving baseline reasoning, so this voice does not argue that models lack useful or advancing capabilities; it argues that those gains remain task-specific and should not be generalized into autonomous-lawyering claims. Material qualifications include vendor-run or proprietary evaluation settings, a low-reliability derivative source whose performance claims remain unverified, and methodological excerpts that provide designs without outcome evidence.

qs.q: From this analysis, three meaningful trends have emerged:  -  Legal work is far from saturated by frontier models**: Under our strict all-pass standard, the frontier models we evaluated complete less than 10% of tasks end-to-end in aggregate.
qs.a: Initial Results on Legal Agent Benchmark: A First Look at Frontier Model Performance on Long-Horizon Legal-Agent Work · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: - Under partial-credit scoring, [Claude Opus 5](/models/anthropic_claude-opus-5) reaches 90.58% weighted pass rate but 55.29% under strict all-pass grading, where every rubric check must pass.
qs.a: Vals Index — Continuous Independent Agentic Benchmark (Legal Sector: Legal Research Bench + Independent HLAB Runs) · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

vlens.an: The selected traditional-law-firm sources support the proposition that benchmark gains demonstrate bounded capability and useful assistance, not dependable autonomous lawyering. Linklaters and Allens report substantial model improvement while finding persistent variation by task, practice area, jurisdiction and configuration, including weaker applied reasoning, incorrect or fictional citations, foreign-law contamination and confidently wrong answers. Their operational conclusion is supervised, task-specific use with expert verification rather than direct reliance. Material variation is chiefly one of scope and emphasis: Allens’ 2024 benchmark stresses the unreliability of then-current general-purpose models; the 2025 Allens and LinksAI studies acknowledge marked progress and a widening role in drafting, summarisation and cross-checking but retain the same reliance boundary. The RAG due-diligence report supports the proposition more indirectly: it documents practical long-context constraints and treats retrieval, embedding and prompt refinements as ongoing or prospective improvements, without testing complete-task success or autonomous legal practice. These curated sources therefore align on the benchmark-to-reliability distinction, although they do not by themselves establish the position of traditional law firms generally.

qs.q: - The average *substance *score of all the LLMs we tested was higher in 2025 (4.3** out of **5**) than in 2024 (**1.92** out of **5**), confirming the overall improvement across the board through the year, including with the appearance of the new generation of reasoning models (such as DeepSeek and OpenAI o1).
qs.a: The 2025 Allens AI Australian law benchmark · Law firms · 2025

qs.q: They do not constitute legal advice and should not be relied on even in situations where they have received a positive mark.
qs.a: The LinksAI English law benchmark (Version 2) · Law firms · 2025

vlens.an: This curated set of market-analysis, consultancy and press sources supports the proposition that headline or average benchmark performance must not be equated with dependable end-to-end legal work. Their common reasoning is that benchmarks test materially different things: bar questions, specialist legal advice, professional work products and complete agentic tasks. They therefore distinguish narrow capability and useful assistance from autonomous practice, stressing persistent legal errors, incomplete or opaque reasoning, citation problems and the resulting need for human verification. They also support task-specific, transparent evaluation through tailored rubrics, sourcing checks and strict all-criteria grading. Material variation concerns emphasis rather than direction: the Descrybe report highlights strong specialised-model results but acknowledges vendor-benchmark and training-exposure limitations; the Linklaters analysis focuses on expert supervision and continuous quality assurance; the BigLaw Bench report develops more practice-specific scoring but attributes superiority claims to Harvey rather than independently validating them; the lawyer-jobs article questions whether even professional benchmarks capture ambiguity and strategic judgment; and Artificial Analysis most directly demonstrates the gap between criterion-level credit and complete-task success through a 14.2% leading all-pass result. These sources do not establish a uniform view among market analysts, consultancies or the press, and several claims remain vendor-produced, interpretive or predictive rather than independently demonstrated.

qs.q: The primary metric we present is the all-pass rate: the share of tasks where all criteria in the rubric are satisfied, reflecting the high standard of real-world professional legal deliverables.
qs.a: Announcing Harvey LAB-AA: evaluating AI agents on real-world legal work · Market & press · 2026

vlens.an:
The curated regulators, courts and professional-bodies sources support the proposition that evidence of narrow capability, speed or strong average benchmark performance does not establish dependable autonomous lawyering. Their common rationale is operational: generated work may be incomplete, inaccurate, outdated or jurisdictionally inapplicable, so lawyers must retain professional judgment, verification and supervision before reliance. Several sources also distinguish demonstrated efficiency from acceptable work-product quality, and one specifically cautions against comparing GPT-5’s Vals score with earlier human-lawyer results without examining whether the tasks and data are comparable.

There is material variation in emphasis. Litigation guidance translates the proposition into concrete checks for court submissions and cautiously prefers specialised legal tools to general-purpose systems. The Victorian census report focuses on the methodological gap between generation speed and speed to an acceptable quality threshold. The GPT-5 discussion scrutinises benchmark comparability while encouraging continued supervised experimentation. Broader sector guidance is comparatively optimistic about GenAI augmenting most legal tasks and improving over time, but still recognises unreliable outputs. Barristers’ guidance extends the practical risk analysis to confidentiality and cybersecurity. LexRubric cannot be positioned substantively because the supplied excerpt is only bibliographic. These differences qualify the scope and implementation of the proposition rather than creating a substantive case against it.

qs.q: I'd want to dig into the data and see exactly what the tasks are and how that compares with those earlier lawyer benchmarks.
qs.a: GPT-5 and the Future of Legal AI Regulation — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2025

elens.an:
The 2023–2024 sources support the proposition’s core distinction between bounded benchmark success, useful legal assistance and dependable autonomous lawyering. Across task benchmarks, practitioner comparisons, legal-advice tests, hallucination research and litigation guidance, the recurring reasons are substantial variation by task and model configuration; weak citation, sourcing and jurisdictional reliability; incomplete coverage of lawyers’ work; and the continuing need for human verification. The period also begins to develop more practice-oriented evaluation through LegalBench, BigLaw Bench, contract review, Australian-law questions, due-diligence extraction and legal-aid intake, moving beyond headline bar-exam results.

Material internal variation concerns the implications rather than the basic evidentiary limits. Some sources emphasise strong capabilities, speed and cost advantages or forecast eventual automation of routine work; Better Call GPT reports near-parity on bounded issue determination, and GPT-4 passes the bar exam describes the model as a legal force multiplier. Others are more sceptical, documenting frequent hallucinations, poor critical reasoning, foreign-law contamination and weak transfer from exams to practice. Harvey’s sources propose richer, task-specific scoring and report product advantages, but those superiority claims are vendor-originated rather than independently established. Re-Regulating UPL in an Age of AI remains unclear because the supplied excerpt invokes bar-exam performance and transformative potential without assessing practical reliability.

These differences do not amount to substantive opposition: even the more optimistic sources generally qualify present performance, distinguish predictions from observed results, or retain human supervision. However, this period does not itself establish the synthesis’s strongest titular claim about strict, end-to-end all-criteria failure; that conclusion depends on later complete-task benchmarks. Because the corpus is curated, this assessment characterises only the supplied sources and does not indicate the prevalence of these views among researchers, firms, courts or practitioners generally.

qs.q: These results emphasize that assessments of LLM capabilities for legal applications must be made on a task-by-task basis, and informed by the nuances of specific tasks.
qs.a: LegalBench: A Collaboratively Built Benchmark for Measuring Legal Reasoning in Large Language Models · Academia · 2023

qs.q: This list of tasks falls far short of the goal of providing a benchmark of all tasks that lawyers must perform to deliver value for their clients.
qs.a: Introducing BigLaw Bench to Evaluate LLMs · Legal-tech vendor · 2024

elens.an: Taken together, the curated 2025 sources support the proposition that improving benchmark and adoption results demonstrate bounded capabilities and useful assistance, not dependable autonomous lawyering. Common reasons are persistent task-specific variation, hallucinations and citation failures, jurisdictional contamination, weak performance on applied or complex reasoning, sensitivity to prompts and configurations, and doubts about whether benchmark graders or exam tasks represent professional work. The operational response is consistently supervised, task-specific deployment with verification, transparent testing and quality controls. Material internal variation concerns emphasis and implication rather than the core finding: PRBench, LeMAJ and the Bluebook study develop more granular evaluation methods; governance sources add confidentiality, cybersecurity and continuous-monitoring concerns; a conceptual proposal advocates verifiable agents; some sources anticipate transformative capacity or possible substitution on basic tasks; and one source redirects attention toward access-to-justice distribution rather than reliability. A specialised-product recommendation remains unclear on the proposition because it supplies no reliability evidence. These differences do not create a balanced case against the proposition, and the selected sources should not be treated as representative of all 2025 commentators or adopters.

qs.q: - The average *substance *score of all the LLMs we tested was higher in 2025 (4.3** out of **5**) than in 2024 (**1.92** out of **5**), confirming the overall improvement across the board through the year, including with the appearance of the new generation of reasoning models (such as DeepSeek and OpenAI o1).
qs.a: The 2025 Allens AI Australian law benchmark · Law firms · 2025

qs.q: Disclaimer  No reliance should be placed on any LLMs or their responses, even in cases where specific answers or LLM performances have been positively marked.
qs.a: The 2025 Allens AI Australian law benchmark · Law firms · 2025

elens.an: The 2026 sources collectively accept the proposition that benchmark success must be interpreted by task, configuration and scoring method, and materially develop it. The strongest direct evidence comes from complete-work-product benchmarks: Harvey’s LAB, Artificial Analysis’s LAB-AA implementation and Vals’ evaluations show that high criterion-level or weighted performance can coexist with much lower all-pass completion. Legora adds a related risk-weighted approach, penalising consequential omissions rather than treating every criterion equally. Other sources extend the proposition beyond completion rates: citation-checking research finds uneven verification across error types; the Thai bar-essay study shows that high LLM-judge agreement can conceal lost interpretive diversity; and research on AI-assisted work distinguishes generation speed or standalone output quality from the performance of humans using AI. Material variation remains. Bounded studies report strong performance on bar questions, selected legal tasks and experimental compliance decisions, but generally do not claim dependable autonomous lawyering. Vendor-run benchmarks require scrutiny for judge-model scoring, possible training-data exposure and configuration dependence; one derivative benchmark is expressly low-reliability, while the LexRubric excerpt is too limited to establish a position. The period therefore strengthens the proposition through new evaluation designs and failure mechanisms rather than showing uniformly weak legal capability. Because the corpus is curated, these relationships should not be read as measuring the prevalence of any view among researchers, vendors or practitioners.
